title: Facilitate negotiations about all aspects of implementing local economic development programmes with a range of relevant stakeholders and role players

lessons.title: Mapping stakeholders in a local economic development programme
lessons.html:
Who has a stake in local economic development?

Local economic development (LED) programmes aim to grow income, jobs and enterprises in a defined area, such as a district municipality or a cluster of villages. In rural South Africa many LED programmes are built around agriculture: a vegetable packhouse, a red meat feedlot for communal farmers, an irrigation scheme revitalisation, or a farmer support centre. The extension officer is often the person asked to bring the parties together and broker agreement.

Before any negotiation, you must know who the role players are and what each one wants. Typical stakeholders include:

  • Local and district municipalities, who own the Integrated Development Plan (IDP) and the LED strategy, and may control land, water connections and roads.
  • Provincial Department of Agriculture, which funds infrastructure, mechanisation and extension support.
  • Traditional authorities, who allocate communal land and carry great influence in rural communities.
  • Farmers, co-operatives and commodity groups, the intended beneficiaries.
  • Private sector partners, such as agri-processors, retailers, input suppliers and banks.
  • Development finance institutions and NGOs, who bring grants, loans or technical expertise.

Analysing interest and influence

A simple tool is the interest-influence grid. Place each stakeholder according to how much they are affected by the programme (interest) and how much they can shape or block it (power). High-power, high-interest players, such as the municipality and the traditional council, must be managed closely and involved in every key decision. High-interest, low-power groups, such as women farmers or youth, must be actively consulted so that their needs are not drowned out.

For each stakeholder, record their stated position (what they say they want) and their underlying interests (why they want it). A traditional council may insist on approving every land lease (position) because it wants to protect community ownership and avoid land loss (interest). Negotiation succeeds when you work with interests, not positions.

Keep a stakeholder register with contact details, mandate, decision-makers, history with the programme and concerns raised. Update it after every meeting. This register becomes the backbone of your negotiation plan.

lessons.title: Preparing and conducting principled negotiations
lessons.html:
Preparation is most of the work

Negotiations about LED implementation cover many aspects: land access, water rights, who contributes what funding, who manages the enterprise, how profits are shared, procurement of local labour and suppliers, timelines, and reporting. Poorly prepared negotiations produce vague agreements that collapse once money starts flowing.

Steps in preparing

  1. Define the issues. List every item that must be agreed, for example the lease period for a 40 ha irrigation block, or the price formula for produce delivered to a packhouse.
  2. Understand each party's mandate. Confirm whether the person at the table can actually commit their organisation. A municipal official may need council approval; a co-operative chair may need a members' resolution.
  3. Identify options. Brainstorm several possible arrangements for each issue before meetings, so the parties are not stuck with a single take-it-or-leave-it proposal.
  4. Know the alternatives. Each party's best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) determines how far they will move. If an agri-processor can easily buy from commercial farmers, the co-operative must offer reliable quality to keep its place.
  5. Gather objective criteria. Market prices, input costs, industry norms and legal requirements give a fair basis for agreement and reduce arguments about opinion.

Facilitating the session

As facilitator you are not the winner or loser. Your role is to keep the process fair and productive. Agree on ground rules at the start: respect, one speaker at a time, confidentiality where needed, and language. Provide interpretation into isiZulu, Sesotho, isiXhosa or other local languages so that farmers participate fully.

Separate the people from the problem. Acknowledge emotions and history, such as past failed projects, but steer discussion back to interests and options. Summarise regularly so that everyone hears what has been agreed. When parties deadlock, use caucuses: meet each side privately to explore what would make an option acceptable.

Watch power imbalances. A large retailer or a government department can dominate small farmers. Ensure farmers have time to consult their members and, where necessary, access to independent advice before they sign.

lessons.title: Recording agreements and managing implementation
lessons.html:
Turning agreement into action

An LED negotiation is only successful when the agreement is implemented. Many rural projects fail not because nobody agreed, but because the agreement was unclear, unwritten or forgotten when officials changed posts.

Documenting the agreement

Record outcomes in writing as soon as possible. Depending on the issue, this may be minutes of a meeting, a memorandum of understanding (MoU), a lease, a supply agreement or a service level agreement. A good agreement states:

  • Each party's responsibilities, contributions and deadlines.
  • Financial arrangements: who pays for what, in rand amounts or formulas, and how funds are controlled.
  • Governance: who sits on the project steering committee and how decisions are made.
  • Indicators of success, such as hectares planted, jobs created or tonnes delivered.
  • A dispute resolution process, for example referral to the steering committee, then to mediation.
  • Review dates and how the agreement can be changed.

Legal agreements involving land, finance or long-term supply should be checked by a legal adviser. Read the final text back to farmer groups in their own language before signing.

Managing ongoing negotiation

Implementation always raises new issues: drought reduces yields, a contractor is late, input prices rise. Treat these as continued negotiation, not as betrayal. Hold regular steering committee meetings, share progress reports openly, and raise problems early.

Maintain relationships between meetings. Phone stakeholders, visit the site with officials and invite the traditional council to field days. Trust built in the field makes formal negotiations easier.

Finally, evaluate the negotiation process. Ask: were all relevant groups included, were agreements realistic, and did benefits reach the intended people? Use these lessons in the next programme.

Key points

  • Map all stakeholders by interest and influence, and keep a stakeholder register.
  • Negotiate on interests, not positions, and use objective criteria such as market prices.
  • Check that each negotiator has a mandate to commit their organisation.
  • Facilitate fairly, provide interpretation and manage power imbalances.
  • Record agreements in writing with responsibilities, finances, indicators and dispute resolution.

quiz.question: In an interest-influence grid, how should a stakeholder with high power and high interest, such as the municipality, be treated?

options.text: Kept informed with occasional newsletters only
Managed closely and involved in every key decision
Ignored until implementation starts
Consulted only if they complain

quiz.question: A traditional council insists on approving every land lease because it wants to protect community ownership. What is the protection of community ownership in this case?

options.text: Its position
Its BATNA
Its underlying interest
Its mandate
Basic agreement to negotiate in advance
Board approval terms for new agreements
Budget allocation towards national agriculture
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement

quiz.question: Two parties are deadlocked during a negotiation session. Which facilitation technique is recommended?

options.text: Hold a caucus with each side privately to explore acceptable options
Let the most powerful party decide
End the programme immediately
Take a vote with all people in the room

quiz.question: Why should you confirm a negotiator's mandate before negotiations?

options.text: To decide who gets lunch first
To know whether that person can actually commit their organisation
To measure their level of education
To exclude farmers from the table

quiz.question: Objective criteria such as market prices and input costs help reduce arguments based on opinion.

options.text: True
False

quiz.question: Once a memorandum of understanding is signed, no further negotiation is needed during implementation.

options.text: True
False

quiz.question: Which items should a good written LED agreement contain? (select all that apply)

options.text: Each party's responsibilities and deadlines
A dispute resolution process
Indicators of success such as jobs created
Personal opinions of the facilitator about each party
A promise that no problems will ever arise
